Checked one (`scribe`'s README) before answering rather than guessing — and it settles the third question directly: **skill→agent diagrams already exist**, every plugin's own README documents its internal pipeline(s) this way (scribe has four — drafting, drift-check, correction, architectural remediation). What's missing isn't the diagrams, it's that they're still in the **pre-refresh style** — `source`/`engine`/`router`/`output` classDefs, 8px radius, 2px stroke, no font-size/weight hierarchy, no legend. A reader who just saw the polished root README would hit a visible downgrade clicking into any plugin.

So, concretely:

1. **Root README** — close to done. Two small real gaps: no link to `docs/adr/007-wisp-persona-naming.md` (a curious reader has no way to find out *why* it's called Weaver/Scribe/etc.), and no link to `CONTRIBUTING.md`. Both are one-line additions.
2. **Individual plugin READMEs** — apply the same visual language we landed on here (category color-coding, shape grammar for checkpoint vs. sequence nodes, font-weight/size hierarchy, legend where an encoding repeats) to all ~10 plugins' existing diagrams. This is mechanical and repetitive across plugins, not a design question anymore — good candidate to delegate rather than do by hand one at a time.
3. **New skill→agent diagrams** — not needed, they already exist; skip this.

Want me to do the two root README link additions now, then delegate the plugin-README diagram refresh as one batched pass?
Let's layout the plugin readmes in the order of importance to users

Good instinct — checked one README's structure, and the current order buries **Install** near the bottom (position 9 of 10) when it should be one of the first things a decided reader needs, and puts deep internals (Pipelines, Subagents) ahead of the actionable Skills table.

My proposed order, by what a reader actually needs at each point:

1. **Title + masthead** (stage/output/version) — what is this
2. **Description** — what it does, in plain terms
3. **When to Use** — decide if this is the right tool
4. **Install** — get unblocked immediately once decided (moved way up)
5. **Skills** — the actionable invocation table
6. **Subagents** — the roster behind those skills, for the curious
7. **Pipelines** — internal diagrams, for those who want the mechanism
8. **Output Schemas** — reference material
9. **Exit Gate Conditions** (where it exists) — reference material
10. **Next Stage** — where to go from here

Biggest move: Install jumps from ~9th to 4th; everything past Skills becomes progressively more "reference," not "decide/act." I'll apply this across all 10 plugin READMEs — since section sets aren't identical everywhere (not every plugin has an Exit Gate Conditions section, some have plugin-specific sections), I'll delegate this as one pass so it can read each file's actual headers and slot them into the right priority zone without dropping or rewriting content.

In the repo /Users/gabe/Projects/agent-plugins, reorder the sections within each of the 10 plugin READMEs (plugins/weaver/README.md, vanguard, scribe, muse, navigator, smith, sentinel, courier, ranger, mason — all under plugins/<id>/README.md) to match this priority order, based on what a reader actually needs at each point in deciding to use and then using the plugin:

1. Title + masthead line (stage/output/version, whatever the plugin currently has at the top)
2. Description (the "what it does" bullets/prose right after the masthead)
3. "When to Use" (trigger phrases / when-to-invoke section)
4. "Install" (currently near the bottom in most of these — move it up to position 4, right after "When to Use")
5. "Skills" (the actionable skill/subagent invocation table)
6. "Subagents" (the agent roster table — tier, model, description)
7. "Pipelines" (mermaid/ASCII diagrams showing internal agent flow)
8. "Output Schemas" (reference material — field tables for produced schemas)
9. Any plugin-specific reference section that exists only in some plugins (e.g. "Exit Gate Conditions", hazard-taxonomy notes, mutation-testing notes) — these are all "reference material for later," so they belong in this zone, between Output Schemas and Next Stage. Use judgment on exact sub-order among these if a plugin has more than one; keep whichever reads most naturally, this isn't a hard rule.
10. "Next Stage" (pointer to what comes after this plugin in the ecosystem) — always last

Rules:
- This is a REORDER task, not a rewrite. Do not change any section's content, wording, tables, or diagrams — only move whole sections (from their header line to just before the next header) to their new position.
- Not every plugin has every section from this list (e.g. a plugin might not have "Exit Gate Conditions" if it doesn't have a binding gate). Skip sections that don't exist; don't invent missing ones.
- Some plugins may have a section that doesn't map cleanly to this list (read each file and use judgment) — place it in whichever priority zone matches its actual purpose: if it's decision-relevant info, keep it early (near items 1-4); if it's reference/internals, place it late (near items 8-9).
- Preserve the `---` horizontal-rule separators between sections exactly as they currently appear between sections (each section is already separated by `---`; keep that convention when you move things around).
- Read each of the 10 files in full before editing it — don't assume they all share scribe's exact structure (scribe is provided here as the reference example already reordered conceptually, but other plugins may have variations, e.g. proof/ranger's README likely documents hazard taxonomy references, lambda/smith's likely documents mutation testing, axiom/sentinel's likely documents the recon→verify→exit-gate protocol itself as a core section rather than an afterthought — use judgment for where that lands, probably early since axiom/sentinel's core section IS its skill essentially).

After reordering all 10, run `./scripts/check-skills-doc.sh` and `./scripts/check-mermaid.sh` to confirm nothing broke (these check structural things like skill-doc accuracy and mermaid validity, not section order, but a botched reorder could accidentally corrupt a mermaid fence or table, so this is a real safety check, not busywork). Report back: for each of the 10 plugins, the section order it ended up with (since not all will be identical), any section that didn't map cleanly to the standard list and where you decided to place it and why, and the validation script output. Do NOT commit anything.

7	## 1. Progressive Disclosure
8

38

40	
41	## 2. Plugin Structure
42	
43	```
44	plugins/<id>/
45	├── plugin.json              ← Manifest: id, version, skills, agents list
46	├── README.md                ← Plugin documentation
47	├── CHANGELOG.md             ← Version history
48	├── skills/<id>/SKILL.md     ← Skill prompt (what the user invokes)
49	└── agents/*.md              ← Individual agent prompts
50	```
51	
52	`plugin.json` fields: `id`, `version` (semver), `description`, `skills` (path to skills dir), `agents` (list of agent file paths).
53	
54	A plugin defaults to one skill directory named after the plugin id. IF the plugin's scope covers several genuinely independent, heterogeneous intents on the same artifact — not a linear pipeline invoked as one flow — `skills/<id>/` may split into `skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` per skill instead; `courier`, `scribe`, `weaver`, and `mason` all do. The routing key is the directory name, not the frontmatter `name:` field. See `shared/constitution.md`'s Plugin Structure and Skill Names sections.
55	
56	---
57	
58	## 3. The Lifecycle Pipeline
59	
60	Ten plugins form a directed pipeline. Each stage produces a typed artifact consumed by the next.
61	
62	```mermaid
63	flowchart LR
64	    classDef source fill:#eef2ff,stroke:#6366f1,stroke-width:2px,color:#1e1b4b,rx:8px,ry:8px;
65	    classDef store fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#0f172a,rx:8px,ry:8px;
66	    classDef engine fill:#f5f3ff,stroke:#8b5cf6,stroke-width:2px,color:#4c1d95,rx:8px,ry:8px;
67	    classDef router fill:#fffbeb,stroke:#f59e0b,stroke-width:2px,color:#78350f,rx:8px,ry:8px;
68	    classDef output fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#10b981,stroke-width:2px,color:#064e3b,rx:8px,ry:8px;
69	    classDef alert fill:#fff1f2,stroke:#f43f5e,stroke-width:2px,color:#881337,rx:8px,ry:8px;
70	
71	    we["**weaver**\nneed"] -->|"requirement@1"| va["**vanguard**\nresearch"]
72	    va -->|"research-report@1"| sc["**scribe**\nspec"]
73	    sc -->|"spec@1"| na["**navigator**\nplan"]
74	    na -->|"plan@1"| sm["**smith**\ncode"]
75	    sm -->|"changeset@2"| co["**courier**"]
76	    co -. iterate .-> we
77	
78	    mu["**muse**\ncomponent spec"] -->|"spec@1"| na
79	
80	    se(["**sentinel**\ngate"])
81	    sc -.->|"spec@1"| se
82	    sm -.->|"changeset@2"| se
83	    se -.->|"verdict@1"| co
84	
85	    ra(["**ranger**\naudit"]) -.->|"finding-report@1"| co
86	    ra -.->|"finding-report@1"| sc
87	    ma(["**mason**\nmeta"]) -. scaffold .-> we
88	
89	    class we source
90	    class va,sc,na,sm,mu engine
91	    class co output
92	    class se router
93	    class ra alert
94	    class ma store
95	```
96	
97	**Composable:** any contiguous subset installs cleanly. Start at `scribe` if requirements come from an external tracker. End at `smith` if automated shipping tooling isn't needed. Layer `sentinel` in at any stage for an independent verification pass.
98	
99	**Substitutable:** any stage can be replaced by a different implementation that honours the same schema contract. A Jira plugin replacing `weaver` just needs to emit `requirement@1`.
100	
101	**Cross-cutting, not inline:** `sentinel`'s `plugin.json` declares `consumes: []` — nothing invokes it automatically. `exit-gate` and `exit-gate` are separate, dedicated agents that independently implement the same recon → verify → judge discipline sentinel formalizes; they do not call into sentinel's own agents. Install sentinel when you want that protocol available standalone against any artifact, including as a second opinion on top of scribe's or smith's own gate.
102	
103	---
104	
105	## 4. Shared Schema Contract
106	
107	Schemas in `shared/schemas/` are the inter-agent API surface. Rules:
108	
109	- **Format:** JSON Schema draft-2020-12
110	- **Strict:** `additionalProperties: false` on all schemas — unknown fields are rejected at validation time
111	- **Scratchpad:** every schema includes `reasoning: string`, an unconstrained chain-of-thought field that is never forwarded downstream
112	- **Immutable versions:** `requirement@1.json` never changes; breaking changes produce `requirement@2.json`
113	- **Validation timing:** wiring time, before agent execution — not at runtime inside the agent
114	
115	---
116	
117	## 5. Model and Effort Tiering
118	
119	Each subagent declares `model` and `effort` in its frontmatter. These are routing hints. Claude Code honours them directly; AGY applies its own model routing and ignores them.
120	
121	```mermaid
122	flowchart TD
123	    classDef store fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#0f172a,rx:8px,ry:8px;
124	    classDef engine fill:#f5f3ff,stroke:#8b5cf6,stroke-width:2px,color:#4c1d95,rx:8px,ry:8px;
125	    classDef router fill:#fffbeb,stroke:#f59e0b,stroke-width:2px,color:#78350f,rx:8px,ry:8px;
126	
127	    H["**haiku · low**
128	    Mechanical — deterministic enumeration
129	    Manifest building, file inventory, commit message writing"]
130	
131	    S["**sonnet · medium**
132	    Analysis — multi-step reasoning
133	    Scanning, drafting, planning, implementing, reviewing"]
134	
135	    O["**opus · high**
136	    Judgment — weighing competing evidence
137	    Adversarial review, exit gates, final verdicts"]
138	
139	    H -. "escalate only when judgment required" .-> S
140	    S -. "escalate only when binding verdict required" .-> O
141	
142	    class H store
143	    class S engine
144	    class O router
145	```
146	
147	Use the lowest tier that produces correct output. Opus is reserved for decisions that produce a binding verdict with downstream consequences.
148	
149	---
150	
151	## 6. The Sentinel Gate Protocol
152	
153	`sentinel` is a reusable, artifact-agnostic verification gate. Any artifact type — spec, plan, changeset, finding report — can be run through it.
154	
155	```mermaid
156	flowchart LR
157	    classDef source fill:#eef2ff,stroke:#6366f1,stroke-width:2px,color:#1e1b4b,rx:8px,ry:8px;
158	    classDef store fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#0f172a,rx:8px,ry:8px;
159	    classDef engine fill:#f5f3ff,stroke:#8b5cf6,stroke-width:2px,color:#4c1d95,rx:8px,ry:8px;
160	    classDef router fill:#fffbeb,stroke:#f59e0b,stroke-width:2px,color:#78350f,rx:8px,ry:8px;
161	    classDef output fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#10b981,stroke-width:2px,color:#064e3b,rx:8px,ry:8px;
162	    classDef alert fill:#fff1f2,stroke:#f43f5e,stroke-width:2px,color:#881337,rx:8px,ry:8px;
163	
164	    Art[artifact + criteria]
165	
166	    subgraph check [Verification Chain]
167	        direction LR
168	        Recon["recon
169	        haiku / low"] --> Ver["verifier
170	        sonnet / medium"] --> Gate["exit-gate
171	        opus / high"]
172	    end
173	
174	    Art --> Recon
175	
176	    Fix["producing agent
177	    targeted patch on blockers
178	    (effort escalates on retry 2)"]
179	
180	    Gate -->|pass| Done(["verdict@1 · pass"])
181	    Gate -->|fail| Fix
182	    Fix -->|"retry ≤ 3 · updated retry_count"| Art
183	    Fix -->|"retry > 3"| Esc(["escalate to human"])
184	
185	    class Art source
186	    class Recon store
187	    class Ver engine
188	    class Gate router
189	    class Done output
190	    class Fix router
191	    class Esc alert
192	
193	    style check fill:#fafafa,stroke:#cbd5e1,stroke-width:1.5px,stroke-dasharray: 4 4,rx:10px,ry:10px
194	```
195	
196	On `fail`, the orchestrator passes **only the blockers array** back to the producing agent — not the full artifact context — so it can make a targeted fix. On retry 2, the effort level escalates. After 3 retries, the circuit breaks and control passes to the human.
197	
198	`retry_count` is tracked inside `verdict@1` and incremented by the exit gate on each pass.
199	
200	---
201	
202	## 7. Agent Authoring Principles
203	
204	Full guide: `shared/agent-best-practices.md`. Key constraints:
205	
206	**5-part agent structure** — every agent defines:
207	
208	| Part | Purpose |
209	| :--- | :--- |
210	| **Constitution** | Ecosystem-wide invariants, byte-identical across every agent — the shared cache prefix. Never authored per-agent; copied verbatim. |
211	| **Backstory** | 2–4 sentences of experiential perspective. What has this agent been burned by? What does it value? Guides judgment in the open interior. |
212	| **Goal** | What the agent must produce and why. Intent, not steps. |
213	| **Judgment** | How to know if the goal was genuinely achieved vs. output that looks like it was. Names the key failure mode. |
214	| **Output** | Structured output shape, referencing a schema from `shared/schemas/` when the output flows to another agent. |
215	
216	**Cognitive mode dispatch** — agents are dispatched by the cognitive mode they require, not their pipeline position.
217	- A scanner (exhaustive pattern matching, no filtering) and an adversary (default-to-skepticism, requires a concrete failing scenario) cannot share a mental mode — combining them produces an agent worse at both
218	- Modes: enumeration (haiku/low), tracing/analysis/repair (sonnet/medium), adversarial judgment (opus/high)
219	- A plugin with distinct scanning, tracing, adversarial, and repair phases has a dedicated agent per mode
220	
221	**Progressive context loading** — each agent loads only the reference file for its cognitive phase.
222	- A `<load_first>` block names the specific `shared/references/` file — scanner loads hazards, architect loads smells, mutator loads tooling
223	- Never load all reference files into all agents — attention degrades when the context window contains material the agent won't use
224	
225	**EARS for edges only** — EARS notation (`WHEN`, `IF`, `WHILE`, `WHERE`) belongs in output contracts and never-do rules.
226	- Not in implementation steps or search strategies — those are the interior where agent judgment is the point
227	- Over-constraining the interior caps the agent at the level of the author's imagination
228	
229	**Schema-driven handoffs** — where one agent's output is another's input, both reference the same schema file from `shared/schemas/`. The schema is the contract; the prompt describes the intent.
230	
231	---
232	
233	## 8. Cross-Platform Compatibility
234	
235	Plugins run natively in Claude Code and AGY — no custom server framework required.
236	
237	| Concern | Approach |
238	| :--- | :--- |
239	| Model routing | `model`/`effort` frontmatter for Claude Code; AGY uses its own router |
240	| Tool calls | Abstract language — portable across both platforms |
241	| Paths | Relative only — `shared` symlink provides consistent paths from any plugin dir |
242	| Schema validation | Wiring-time, host-side — agents never validate JSON Schema directly |
243

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page - what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is not part of this read: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it - a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first - CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world - its materials, instruments, vernacular - is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits - link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject - the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* - most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token - a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first - don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme - then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content - tables, code, diagrams - gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly - their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out - a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen - name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it - no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject - or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name - a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word - a greeting, a category, a page-type label - the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number - a pill, a chip, a severity stripe - so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan - a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4-6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles - a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world - headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

# Wisp — Design Brief ## What it is **Wisp** is the umbrella brand for a 10-plugin Claude Code / AGY ecosystem (repo: `orin-dx/agent-plugins`) that helps developers build non-trivial software with AI coding agents without silently dropping requirements as context compresses. The core mechanic: every stage of the dev lifecycle (requirements → research → spec → plan → implementation → verification → shipping) is handled by a specialized plugin that reads/writes typed, versioned artifacts to disk — specs live on disk, agents read from disk, drift is detectable instead of silent. **Audience:** software engineers, mostly senior/technical, installing this inside Claude Code. The tone needs to read as *credible professional tooling* — not enterprise-cold, but also not cartoonish or twee. ## The naming philosophy — why "Wisp" The 10 plugins used to be named after abstract math/logic nouns (axiom, basis, canon, delta, graph, lambda, proof, trace, vector) — technically elegant, but memorability became a real cost once the ecosystem passed 9 plugins. The fix: rename every plugin to a **persona** — a character with an obvious craft — and split "who" (the plugin, a character) from "what" (the skill, a literal action), so an invocation like `sentinel:gate` or `smith:implement` is self-explanatory without memorizing a lookup table. The umbrella name **Wisp** was chosen deliberately from folklore: a *will-o'-the-wisp* is a small, wandering light that leads travelers through uncertain ground in the dark. That's the actual metaphor for the product — each persona is a small guiding light that takes a different shape for a different part of the journey from raw idea to shipped code. It's meant to feel warm, a little magical, and *helpful* — not a cold "AI assistant" glow. Names explicitly rejected along the way, for calibration: `Prism` (collides with another of the founder's own tools), `Guild`/`Forge`/`Atelier`/`Loft`/`Den` (umbrella-name candidates that felt too generic or too try-hard), `Hachi`/`Apis`/`Agora`/`Numen`/`Genii`/`Lares` (too scholarly/dry for the individual persona names), and naming plugins after real famous engineers (a pattern already used elsewhere by this team, deliberately avoided here to stay distinct). ## The ten personas | Category | Persona | Job | |---|---|---| | Define | **Weaver** | Turns scattered raw need into structured requirements | | Define | **Vanguard** | Goes first — researches prior art and risk before anyone commits to a direction | | Design | **Scribe** | Drafts and gates the authoritative, testable spec | | Design | **Muse** | Specs and audits UI components — props, states, accessibility | | Build | **Navigator** | Sequences the spec into an exact, step-by-step plan | | Build | **Smith** | Implements via TDD — failing test, minimal code, green, commit | | Verify | **Sentinel** | Cross-cutting gate — confirms any artifact meets its criteria | | Verify | **Ranger** | Hunts down real bugs through adversarial verification | | Ship | **Courier** | Carries finished work through commit, PR, and release | | Meta | **Mason** | Lays the foundation — scaffolds and audits every other plugin (stands outside the sequence) | Five of these categories form a linear pipeline (Define → Design → Build → Verify → Ship); Mason sits apart, maintaining the family itself rather than being a stage in it. ## What's wrong with the current logo `assets/logo.svg` is a cold cyan/blue "AI tech emblem" — neon glow filters, gradient nodes, a bold all-caps geometric sans wordmark ("ORIN AGENT PLUGINS"). It reads as a generic AI-startup mark and has zero connection to the wisp/guiding-light concept the whole brand is now built around. ## Constraints for the new logo - **Must survive both a white and a near-black GitHub README background.** GitHub does not reliably run CSS `prefers-color-scheme` media queries inside an ``-embedded SVG, so the real deliverable is two files (light-tuned, dark-tuned) served through a `` element — not one SVG trying to self-adapt. - **Avoid the current "AI-generated design" clichés**: purple-to-blue gradient hero glow, neon-emblem tech look, Inter/Space Grotesk as the "safe" display face, generic rounded-lg treatment. - **Warm, not cold.** Ember/candlelight energy — a guiding light over uncertain ground — rather than a sterile blue "AI" glow. - **Credible, not cutesy.** No ghost mascots, no fantasy/wizard-kitsch lettering. This is developer tooling first. - **Should scale down cleanly** — used as a masthead lockup around 300–400px wide, ideally also legible at favicon scale. ## Directions already explored (for calibration, not to be repeated verbatim) Three concepts were drafted and shown to the founder as an Artifact — reactions not yet finalized, but useful signal on the target territory: 1. **Ember Trail** — a single flame shape mid-flicker with a soft curling tail. Most literal to the folklore. 2. **Twin Light** — two small glowing points (one warm, one cool) drifting on a faint shared arc, symbolizing "a family of many small guiding personas" rather than one flame. 3. **Drift Mark** — a minimal line trailing off into a single point of light. Most abstract, most likely to survive at tiny scale. Palette used in the drafts (a starting point, not locked): warm ember gold (`#FFCB7D` → `#D9791F`), a muted dusk violet (`#6E5B9E`) as the cool counterpoint, and warm off-black/off-white neutrals (`#241E2C` / `#F1EBE2`) rather than pure grey. Wordmark was set in **Fraunces** (a warm, slightly literary serif) instead of a geometric sans, with small tracked-caps captions in **IBM Plex Mono** for a technical grounding note. *Note: the README's own internal diagrams use a separate, cooler categorical palette (indigo/violet/blue/amber/emerald/slate, one hue per lifecycle category) for functional color-coding — that system is unrelated to the logo and shouldn't be reused for it; the logo needs its own distinct warm identity.*

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Extracts every ```mermaid fenced block from every .md file in the repo and
# renders each through @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli. Reports which files/blocks
# fail to parse — a diagram with a syntax error still displays as valid
# markdown, so `git status`/`jq`-style checks never catch this; only an
# actual render does. Needs Node (npx); no repo dependency required, resolved
# on demand.
#
# Usage: scripts/check-mermaid.sh

set -euo pipefail
script_dir="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
# shellcheck source=lib/report.sh
source "$script_dir/lib/report.sh"
cd "$script_dir/.."

workdir="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf "$workdir"' EXIT

fail=0
count=0

while IFS= read -r -d '' file; do
  block_index=0
  in_block=0
  block_content=""
  while IFS= read -r line; do
    if [[ "$line" == '```mermaid' ]]; then
      in_block=1
      block_content=""
      continue
    fi
    if [[ $in_block -eq 1 && "$line" == '```' ]]; then
      in_block=0
      count=$((count + 1))
      mmd="$workdir/block_${count}.mmd"
      printf '%s\n' "$block_content" > "$mmd"
      if ! npx --yes @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli -i "$mmd" -o "$workdir/block_${count}.svg" > "$workdir/log_${count}.txt" 2>&1; then
        fail=$((fail + 1))
        echo "FAIL: $file (block $((block_index + 1)))"

So this isn't a regression from our rename — it's a pre-existing, unrelated bug: `check-mermaid.sh` shells out to `@mermaid-js/mermaid-cli`, which launches a headless Chrome via Puppeteer. GitHub Actions runners run jobs as root, and Chrome refuses to start its sandbox as root without an explicit `--no-sandbox` flag — the workflow never passes one, so every single diagram in the repo fails identically, regardless of content. Worth fixing since it's currently blocking every PR that touches any markdown file, not just ours.

**CI passes now** — `validate` went green (1m3s). Root cause was confirmed to be exactly what I suspected: a pre-existing, unrelated bug where GitHub Actions' root-user runner can't launch Chrome's sandbox for `mermaid-cli`'s Puppeteer, which had been failing on `main` for at least 5 prior runs before this PR even existed. Fixed by passing `--no-sandbox` in CI only, scoped so it doesn't disturb your local dev setup (where a custom puppeteer config was interfering with an already-cached Chrome binary for an unrelated reason). Caught and fixed a real bug in my own first attempt along the way — macOS's bash 3.2 throws on empty-array expansion under `set -u`, which would've broken local usage entirely if I'd shipped it as-is.

PR https://github.com/orin-dx/agent-plugins/pull/1 is green and ready for your review.

plugins/muse/agents/drafter.md:18:I've watched component specs pass review that described a button and left the important decisions to whoever built it. Three weeks later the accessibility audit failed and nobody could agree whether it was a bug or an unstated requirement. The failure mode I've learned to hunt is surface completeness: a spec that lists every prop and variant but never says what the component does, observably, in each state a real user or assistive technology will actually encounter. My job is to name every state and every accessibility criterion as a testable proposition before a single line of markup gets written.
plugins/muse/agents/drafter.md:22:Produce a spec@1 from a requirement@1 (or design intent) that gives a developer everything needed to implement the component without asking a clarifying question. Invalid prop combinations must be named explicitly as error cases rather than left to silent implementation choice. In correction mode, read the existing spec from spec_file_path, locate the criterion named by criterion_id, and rewrite it so that the corrected criterion is confirmable against the observed behavior in the contradiction report rather than the disproven original claim — check whether any other criterion depended on the original claim and revise those too, then return the complete spec object with revision_note describing what changed and why.
plugins/muse/agents/drafter.md:26:A component spec is genuinely complete when every acceptance criterion can be confirmed true or false by a tester who has never seen the implementation — using only observable behavior (rendered markup, computed accessibility role/name, focus behavior, emitted events), no knowledge of how the component is implemented internally. When specifying `api_surface` prop signatures for an existing component family or design-system convention, inspect the live source or design-system reference in the workspace first rather than approximating names from memory. The key failure mode is the semantic model anti-pattern: a criterion that sounds concrete but encodes an implementation assumption. "The disabled state looks disabled" is not a criterion — it is a task description. "When `disabled` is true, the element carries `aria-disabled=\"true\"`, is removed from the tab order, and emits no `onClick`" is a criterion. A second failure mode specific to components: silently leaving one interactive state unspecified because it seemed obvious. Every state named in the requirement — and every state a stateful control conventionally has (focus, disabled, loading, error, empty) — needs its own criterion or an explicit non_goal saying it's out of scope. The test: could two competent developers, working independently with no knowledge of the implementation, evaluate the criterion from identical observable behavior, in every state? If not, the criterion is not done.

input.description: Research WCAG and machine-checkable a11y rules
input.prompt:
Research WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) for the purpose of informing how an AI coding-agent pipeline should draft accessibility requirements and scan code for accessibility defects.

Cover, with real sources (search the web, don't rely on memory alone):
1. WCAG 2.2's structure: the four POUR principles (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust), the three conformance levels (A/AA/AAA), and roughly how many success criteria exist at each level.
2. Which WCAG success criteria are most commonly automatable/machine-checkable (e.g., via axe-core, Lighthouse, pa11y) versus which genuinely require human judgment — this distinction matters because a coding agent can reliably scan for some things (missing alt text, color contrast ratios, missing form labels, heading order) but not others (whether alt text is meaningfully descriptive, whether a workflow is genuinely understandable).
3. How major automated accessibility testing tools (axe-core/Deque, Lighthouse, pa11y, WAVE) structure their rule definitions — look at the actual shape of an axe-core rule (id, description, WCAG success criterion mapping, impact level, selector/matching logic) since this is a good model for how we might define a similar "hazard taxonomy" rule format.
4. WCAG 3.0 (formerly "Silver") — what's different about its draft approach (outcomes-based scoring vs pass/fail) and whether it's stable enough to plan against yet, or still too early-draft.
5. Any recent (2025/2026) guidance specifically about using LLMs/AI agents for accessibility auditing or accessible-by-default code generation — search for this specifically, it's a fast-moving area.

Return a structured findings report: a summary of WCAG's structure usable by someone unfamiliar with it, a list of the most machine-checkable success criteria with their SC numbers (e.g. 1.1.1, 1.4.3, 4.1.2) and what an automated check for each would concretely look for, the axe-core rule shape as a model, and anything found on LLM-assisted a11y auditing. Cite sources.

input.description: Research BBC, NN/g, and leading a11y/UX experts
input.prompt:
Research how leading, widely-respected organizations and practitioners approach accessibility as a design discipline (not just a compliance checklist), for the purpose of informing how an AI coding-agent pipeline should think about accessibility during spec-writing and design, not just code auditing.

Cover, with real sources (search the web, don't rely on memory alone):
1. BBC's accessibility standards and guidelines (they publish "BBC Accessibility Standards and Guidelines" and have historically been a widely-cited public example of an org treating a11y as a first-class product requirement, not an afterthought — find their actual current guidance, and anything about their process for baking accessibility into design/spec stages before code is written).
2. Nielsen Norman Group (NN/g)'s published research and articles on accessibility, specifically anything framing accessibility as inseparable from good UX (search for terms like "accessibility usability", "inclusive design", NN/g's accessibility research reports) — what's their core argument for why accessible design produces better design for everyone, and what process guidance do they give for incorporating accessibility from the start of a design process rather than retrofitting it.
3. Other widely-cited accessibility/inclusive-design practitioners and their core frameworks: Microsoft's Inclusive Design Toolkit/principles, Heydon Pickering's "Inclusive Components" approach, the A11Y Project's checklist philosophy, WebAIM's practical guidance, and any well-known "accessibility acceptance criteria" or "definition of done" templates used by real engineering teams (search for "accessibility acceptance criteria template", "accessibility definition of done").
4. Specifically look for any guidance on writing accessibility requirements as testable/falsifiable acceptance criteria (as opposed to vague statements like "must be accessible") — this is the exact shape we need since our spec-drafting agents require every acceptance criterion to be a testable proposition.

Return a structured findings report covering each source's core contribution, with a focus on: (a) how to write accessibility as testable acceptance criteria at spec time, (b) how to treat accessibility as inseparable from UX quality rather than a compliance bolt-on, (c) any concrete checklists or rule-sets that could inform an agent's judgment. Cite sources.

input.description: Research CLI and terminal accessibility
input.prompt:
Research accessibility specifically for command-line interfaces and terminal applications (NOT web/GUI accessibility — that's covered by a separate research effort). This is a less mainstream area; do real web research rather than relying on memory.

Cover, with real sources:
1. Screen reader compatibility with terminal emulators and CLI tools — what actually breaks (e.g., spinners/progress bars that spam a screen reader, ANSI escape codes read aloud as garbage, TUI applications using ncurses-style full-screen rendering that screen readers can't parse, color-only status signaling).
2. The Command Line Interface Guidelines (clig.dev) — what do they say, if anything, about accessibility, output design for non-visual consumption, and machine-readable output modes.
3. The NO_COLOR movement (no-color.org) and related conventions (FORCE_COLOR, terminal capability detection) — the actual convention and why it matters for both accessibility and scriptability.
4. Known best practices for accessible CLI/TUI design: structured/parseable output modes (--json, --plain), avoiding color as the only signal (also pairing with text/symbols), respecting terminal width and NO_COLOR, providing --help and man pages for discoverability, avoiding interactive-only prompts that block non-interactive or assistive-technology use, exit code conventions, avoiding ASCII art/decorative box-drawing that confuses screen readers, and general "output should degrade gracefully when piped or redirected."
5. Search for any published research, blog posts, or conference talks specifically about "CLI accessibility" or "terminal accessibility" or "accessible developer tools" from 2023-2026 — this is a niche but real area (e.g. look for work from GitHub CLI, terminal accessibility working groups, or accessibility-focused devtool teams).
6. Any known frameworks/libraries for building accessible TUIs (e.g. Textual's accessibility features, accessible terminal UI toolkits).

Return a structured findings report: concrete, checkable rules for CLI accessibility (analogous to WCAG success criteria but for terminal interfaces), citing real sources. Be honest about where this area lacks a formal standard (unlike WCAG for web) and what the closest thing to consensus best practice looks like.

Three research threads running in parallel:

1. **WCAG structure + machine-checkable rules** — POUR principles, which success criteria are actually automatable (vs. requiring human judgment), and the axe-core rule shape as a model for our own hazard-taxonomy format.
2. **BBC, NN/g, and leading a11y/UX practitioners** — how they frame accessibility as inseparable from good UX rather than a compliance bolt-on, and how to write accessibility as testable acceptance criteria (matching our own spec-drafting requirement that every criterion be falsifiable).
3. **CLI/terminal accessibility** — a genuinely less-standardized area, covering screen reader compatibility with terminals, `NO_COLOR`, structured/machine-readable output modes, and what the closest thing to consensus best practice looks like.

I already confirmed the internal gap directly (Muse has real a11y depth at the component-spec level; Ranger has zero code-level a11y scanning; Scribe/general specs have no a11y prompting; CLI a11y doesn't exist anywhere in the repo). Once the research lands, I'll write the full report and proposal.

## WCAG Research Findings Report

### 1. WCAG 2.2 structure

WCAG's requirements are organized under four principles, **POUR**:
- **Perceivable** — information/UI must be presentable in ways users can perceive (text alternatives, captions, contrast, adaptable presentation)
- **Operable** — UI and navigation must be operable (keyboard access, timing, seizure avoidance, navigability, input modalities)
- **Understandable** — content and operation must be understandable (readable text, predictable behavior, input assistance)
- **Robust** — content must work with a wide range of current and future user agents/assistive tech (valid parsing, name/role/value exposure)

Three cumulative **conformance levels**: A (minimum) → AA (the level almost all legal mandates, e.g. ADA/EN 301 549, require) → AAA (highest, rarely required site-wide).

**WCAG 2.2 has 86 total success criteria**: 31 at Level A, 24 at Level AA, 31 at Level AAA. Because conformance is cumulative, "AA conformance" = all 31 A criteria + all 24 AA criteria = 55 criteria total. ([W3C WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/), [TestParty — 87 SC breakdown](https://testparty.ai/blog/wcag-22-success-criteria-list), [Eye-Able](https://eye-able.com/blog/wcag-a-aa-aaa))

### 2. Automatable vs. judgment-required criteria

Consistent estimate across sources: **roughly 30–40% of WCAG success criteria are reliably machine-checkable**; the rest need a human. Deque's own volume-weighted analysis claims ~57% of *issue instances* (not SCs) are caught by automation — a higher number because a few automatable rules (contrast, alt presence) fire very frequently in the wild — but by *success-criterion* count the automatable fraction is much smaller, and **no SC required for AA can be fully satisfied by automated testing alone** (Deque itself states this). ([Deque WCAG 2.1 support blog](https://www.deque.com/blog/support-for-wcag-2-1-in-axe-core/), [UK Intelligence Community Design System — automated testing limitations](https://design.sis.gov.uk/accessibility/testing/automated-testing-limitation/))

**Most machine-checkable success criteria** (what an automated check concretely looks for):

| SC | Name | What an automated check looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **1.1.1** | Non-text Content | `<img>`/`area`/`input[type=image]` missing `alt` attribute, or empty `alt` on a non-decorative-looking image (presence only — *not* whether the alt text is meaningful) |
| **1.3.1** | Info and Relationships | Missing table headers (`<th>`/`scope`), missing `<label for>`/`aria-label` on form controls, heading level skips (h1→h3), list markup misuse |
| **1.4.3** | Contrast (Minimum) | Computed foreground/background color luminance ratio < 4.5:1 (or 3:1 for large text) — fully algorithmic |
| **1.4.4 / 1.4.10** | Resize Text / Reflow | Fixed px units preventing 200% zoom without horizontal scroll, viewport meta blocking zoom |
| **2.1.1 / 2.4.3** | Keyboard / Focus Order | Elements with `tabindex` > 0, positive tabindex misuse, `onclick` on non-interactive elements with no keyboard handler |
| **2.4.2** | Page Titled | Missing/empty `<title>` |
| **2.4.4 / 2.4.9** | Link Purpose | Empty link text, generic text like "click here" with no accessible name, duplicate link text pointing to different destinations |
| **3.1.1** | Language of Page | Missing/invalid `lang` attribute on `<html>` |
| **4.1.1** | Parsing (deprecated in 2.2 but still checked) | Duplicate IDs, unclosed/malformed tags |
| **4.1.2** | Name, Role, Value | Custom widgets/ARIA roles missing required name/role/state (e.g., `role="button"` with no accessible name), invalid ARIA attribute values, ARIA on unsupported elements |

**Requires human judgment (cannot be reliably automated):**
- Whether alt text is *meaningfully descriptive* vs. just present (1.1.1)
- Whether reading order and focus order make logical *sense* (1.3.2, 2.4.3)
- Whether a workflow, instructions, or error message is genuinely *understandable* (3.3.x, 3.1.5)
- Whether content requiring user input has adequate context/help (3.3.5)
- Meaningful sequence and purpose of gestures/motion (2.5.x)
- Whether captions/audio descriptions are accurate (1.2.x)
- Consistent navigation and identification *in a meaningful sense* (3.2.3/3.2.4) — structurally checkable but semantically judged

### 3. Automated tool rule structures

**axe-core (Deque)** — the most detailed public model. A rule is JSON with: `id`, `impact` (minor/serious/critical, sometimes "moderate"), `selector` (CSS/DOM-path matcher), `matches` (a named function for extra filtering logic beyond the selector), `tags` (WCAG SC mapping like `wcag2aa`, `wcag143`, plus `EN-301-549`, `ACT`, best-practice tags), `actIds` (links to W3C ACT test rules), `metadata.description` / `metadata.help` (human-readable explanation), and `all`/`any`/`none` arrays of atomic **checks** that combine to a pass/fail. Real example (`color-contrast.json`):

```json
{
  "id": "color-contrast",
  "impact": "serious",
  "matches": "color-contrast-matches",
  "excludeHidden": false,
  "tags": ["cat.color", "wcag2aa", "wcag143", "TTv5", "TT13.c",
           "EN-301-549", "EN-9.1.4.3", "ACT", "RGAAv4", "RGAA-3.2.1"],
  "actIds": ["afw4f7", "09o5cg"],
  "metadata": {
    "description": "Ensure the contrast between foreground and background colors meets WCAG 2 AA minimum contrast ratio thresholds",
    "help": "Elements must meet minimum color contrast ratio thresholds"
  },
  "all": [],
  "any": ["color-contrast"],
  "none": []
}
```
This id→impact→WCAG-SC-tag→description→matcher-logic shape is a strong direct model for a "hazard taxonomy" entry: taxonomy_id, severity, SC mapping(s), human-readable description, and a matching/detection rule. ([axe-core rule-development.md](https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core/blob/master/doc/rule-development.md), [color-contrast.json](https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core/blob/develop/lib/rules/color-contrast.json))

**pa11y** is a runner, not its own engine — it drives headless Chrome via Puppeteer and delegates rule evaluation to a pluggable engine, either **axe-core** or **HTML_CodeSniffer** (WCAG2/Section 508 rulesets); it adds orchestration (CLI/CI config, `pa11y.json`, `--ignore`/`--threshold` flags) but no rules of its own. ([pa11y GitHub](https://github.com/pa11y/pa11y))

**Lighthouse** (Google) wraps axe-core-derived audits into its accessibility category, scoring 0–100 and grouping by impact.

**WAVE** (WebAIM) uses its own proprietary rule engine with icon-based annotations (errors, alerts, features, structural elements, ARIA) overlaid directly on the rendered page rather than a JSON rule export.

### 4. WCAG 3.0 ("Silver")

Still an **early-stage W3C Working Draft** — not stable enough to plan against yet:
- Latest Working Draft published **September 2025** (updated March 2026); explicitly **not a Recommendation** and not to be used for compliance.
- Replaces binary pass/fail SCs with an **outcomes-based scoring model**: each of **174 outcomes** (vs. 86 SCs in 2.2) is scored 0–4 rather than pass/fail.
- Replaces A/AA/AAA with **Bronze/Silver/Gold** conformance; Bronze requires an average score ≥3.5 across all outcomes with the same floor in every functional category.
- Timeline: Candidate Recommendation expected ~late 2027, final publication targeted ~late 2029.
- No law anywhere currently references WCAG 3.0; WCAG 2.x remains the compliance target for the foreseeable future — **do not architect the pipeline around WCAG 3.0's schema yet**, but the outcomes/scoring shift is worth tracking since it changes "pass/fail" into a graded score, which may map better onto an LLM-based hazard-confidence model. ([WCAG 3.0 explainer — webability.io](https://www.webability.io/blog/wcag-3-0-explained), [web-accessibility-checker.com preparation guide](https://web-accessibility-checker.com/en/blog/wcag-3-0-preparation-guide), [accessibility.com — First Public Working Draft](https://www.accessibility.com/blog/silver-wcag-3-0-first-public-working-draft-released))

### 5. LLM/AI-agent accessibility auditing — recent (2025/2026) findings

This is genuinely fast-moving and directly relevant:

- **Microsoft's A11y LLM Eval** (2025/2026, tests GPT-5.x, Claude Haiku/Opus/Sonnet, Gemini 3.x on 32 accessibility test cases across React/Vanilla JS): **baseline LLM-generated code passes only ~12%** of accessibility checks with no guidance; giving models a detailed WCAG 2.2 instruction set raises the pass rate to **~60%** (a 48.5-point jump). Even minimal instructions help (37%). Most common residual failures: color contrast (89% of detected issues), missing ARIA attributes/roles, broken focus management in interactive widgets, and missing helper-text associations. Complex layouts (e.g., shopping pages) scored 0% across all models — implying an agent pipeline needs explicit, structured a11y requirements injected at generation time, not reliance on default model behavior. ([microsoft.github.io/a11y-llm-eval-report](https://microsoft.github.io/a11y-llm-eval-report/))

- **CodeA11y** (CHI 2025, arXiv 2502.10884) — a GitHub Copilot extension using three cooperating LLM agents: a **Responder** (generates accessible code proactively from a system prompt tuned to a11y standards), a **Correction agent** (parses axe DevTools linter output and proposes fixes), and a **Reminder agent** (flags manual-check-only items, e.g. meaningful alt text, that automation can't verify). This maps closely onto a coding-agent pipeline design: generate-with-guidance → automated-scan → LLM-mediated-fix-suggestion → flag-for-human-review on judgment items. Finding: LLM-assisted code can match or exceed human-written accessibility in some cases but still fails on compliance depth; novice developers using AI assistants still omit key practices. ([CodeA11y paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2502.10884), [CHI 2025 ACM record](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3706598.3713335))

- **A11yN** ("aligning LLMs for accessible web UI code generation") — trains/aligns a code-generating LLM via a reward function that penalizes WCAG violations, with penalty severity scaled to violation severity as scored by an accessibility testing engine (i.e., RL/DPO-style alignment against axe-core-style scoring, not just prompting).

- **A11YRepair** (arXiv 2606.21926, "knowledge-enhanced divide-and-conquer repair") and the related "Blind Edits to Verified Repair" work (arXiv 2608.24913) converge on the same architecture recommendation: **never let an LLM patch blind** — apply candidate fix → re-run an automated auditor (axe-core plus computed-style probes) → accept only if detected violations strictly decrease → otherwise roll back and reprompt with the specific violation findings as feedback. This "generate → scan → gate → loop" pattern is the clearest concrete blueprint found for how a coding-agent pipeline should structure its accessibility remediation loop.

- General 2026 framing: audits still find **>90% of public web pages contain detectable violations**; the consensus across these papers is that AI hasn't replaced accessibility specialists but "made their expertise scalable" — i.e., automation should surface candidates and human/specialist judgment should remain the gate for anything above the machine-checkable ~30–40% of criteria.

### Implication for pipeline design

- **Requirements drafting**: for each generated component, inject the machine-checkable SC list (1.1.1 presence, 1.3.1 structure, 1.4.3 contrast, 2.4.2 title, 4.1.2 name/role/value, etc.) as concrete, falsifiable generation constraints — this is what took Microsoft's eval from 12%→60%.
- **Scanning**: model the hazard taxonomy directly on axe-core's rule shape (id, impact, SC-tag, description, matcher) — it's already a proven, widely-adopted format and would let the pipeline optionally shell out to real axe-core/pa11y for the machine-checkable half rather than reinventing detection logic.
- **Judgment items**: don't let the scanner claim confidence on alt-text quality, workflow understandability, or meaningful reading order — flag these explicitly as "needs human/specialist review," mirroring CodeA11y's Reminder agent and A11y LLM Eval's finding that passing automated checks doesn't guarantee WCAG conformance.
- **Repair loop**: adopt the generate→scan→gate(strictly-decreasing-violations)→rollback-and-reprompt pattern from A11YRepair rather than one-shot fixes.</result>

## Findings Report: Accessibility as a Design Discipline (for Spec-Time Reasoning)

### 1. BBC — Accessibility Design Review (pre-code process)

BBC's practice is documented publicly at [bbc.github.io/accessibility-news-and-you](https://bbc.github.io/accessibility-news-and-you/guides/accessibility-design-review.html) (repo: [bbc/accessibility-news-and-you](https://github.com/bbc/accessibility-news-and-you/blob/master/accessibility-news-and-designers.md)) plus their formal [BBC Mobile Accessibility Standards and Guidelines](https://www.usabilityinciviclife.org/bibliography/bbc-mobile-accessibility-standards-and-guidelines-v1-0/) and a current supplier framework for accessibility consultancy/review effective Jan 2025 ([find-tender.service.gov.uk notice](https://www.find-tender.service.gov.uk/Notice/001914-2025/PDF)).

Key mechanism — a **structured design review that happens before sign-off, before any code**:
- An "accessibility champion" (any discipline, not necessarily an a11y specialist) pairs with the designer for 1–2 hours per component.
- Five-step review: visual inspection → check against key user-group considerations → compare against known best-practice references (e.g., Home Office Digital / Barclays accessibility posters) → verify user research included participants with access needs → **write out the intended screen-reader experience narrative** for the component.
- That screen-reader narrative is the deliverable that crosses the design→dev boundary — it tells developers what semantics/behavior to build to, before a line of code exists.
- Designer's own checklist requires, at design time: standard link/focus/hover states; 4.5:1 contrast (tool-checked); color-blindness simulation; explicit decision on whether icons need visually-hidden text; explicit call on heading structure/ARIA landmarks (discussed *with* developers pre-build); logical tab order; and an explicit answer to "does this degrade gracefully without JS."

**Relevance to spec-writing agents**: BBC's model proves the "screen reader experience script" is a legitimate, testable spec artifact — a designer/spec-writer states expected role/name/state announcements before implementation, which is directly falsifiable later against actual AT output.

### 2. Nielsen Norman Group — accessibility as inseparable from UX quality

Sources: [NN/g Accessibility and Inclusivity: Study Guide](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/accessibility-inclusivity-study-guide/), [NN/g accessibility topic/reports hub](https://www.nngroup.com/reports/topic/accessibility/), [Beyond Accessibility: Treating Users with Disabilities as People](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/beyond-accessibility-treating-users-with-disabilities-as-people/), [Inclusive Design: Part 2](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/inclusive-design-part-2/).

Core argument: NN/g explicitly frames **accessibility and inclusivity as branches of usability, not compliance categories** — "mindsets rather than collections of procedures, regulations, or checklists." Their stated rationale for why accessible design is just better design: features built for access needs (contrast, clear labeling, keyboard operability, predictable structure) measurably help everyone, not only disabled users — captured in their framing "accessible solutions benefit everyone." They cite population scale (an estimated 15–20% of people live with a disability, and a similar proportion is neurodiverse) as the business/design case for treating this as core UX, not edge-case handling.

Process guidance for starting-early rather than retrofitting: (a) test with actual users with disabilities early, not just automated/heuristic checks — "the only way to know if designs are accessible and usable... is to test them with this population"; (b) NN/g's "Beyond Accessibility" piece pushes teams to treat disabled users as people with goals and context, not a checkbox demographic, which argues for accessibility being part of persona/scenario work at the requirements stage, not appended later; (c) inclusive design should start at the "organizational"/planning level (Part 2, drawing on Tognazzini) — embedded in foundational project structure rather than bolted onto a finished design.

**Relevance**: Justifies a design principle for the pipeline: accessibility considerations belong in the same acceptance-criteria pass as any other UX quality bar — not a separate "a11y section" appended afterward — and that criteria should reference real assistive-tech user validation, not just automated-checker pass/fail, wherever feasible.

### 3. Other frameworks and practitioner sources

- **Microsoft Inclusive Design Toolkit** ([inclusive.microsoft.design](https://inclusive.microsoft.design/), [Inclusive 101 guidebook](https://inclusive.microsoft.design/articles/inclusive-101-guidebook)): three core principles — *recognize exclusion; learn from diversity; solve for one, extend to many*. The 2nd-edition toolkit (design-for-cognition) adds: understand user motivation/goals/tasks; assess cognitive load of the mismatch; co-create with a diverse community. Trained ~80,000 Microsoft employees and taught at 60+ universities — a widely-adopted framework for translating "who is excluded by this design decision" into an explicit design-time question, which maps well onto asking a spec-writing agent to state, per feature, who could be excluded and how the spec addresses it.

- **Heydon Pickering, Inclusive Components** ([book.inclusive-components.design](https://book.inclusive-components.design/)): philosophy is "not about wrong and right, but bad to better" — a pragmatic, non-perfectionist stance. Approach: examine one component at a time, ask who could be tripped up by it, and prefer semantic HTML + native behavior over custom JS reimplementation. Explicitly names the tension between logical document structure, visual layout, and interaction, and says compromise is inevitable but "should be an equitable sort of compromise" — useful framing for an agent judging trade-offs rather than treating a11y as pass/fail absolutist.

- **The A11Y Project checklist** ([a11yproject.com/checklist](https://www.a11yproject.com/checklist/)): built directly on WCAG as shared vocabulary, targets AA, and is explicit that "there is no such thing as 100% accessible" — the checklist is a floor for continuous improvement, not a certificate. Values noted: person-first/non-ableist language, and verifying with actual daily AT users, not just automated tooling.

- **WebAIM** ([webaim.org/standards/wcag/checklist](https://webaim.org/standards/wcag/checklist), [WCAG testability](https://webaim.org/blog/wcag-2-testability/)): translates WCAG's formal success criteria into plain-language, verifiable checks organized by the four POUR principles (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust). Important structural point: **WCAG itself defines "testable" formally** — a criterion must be answerable "yes/no" by a machine, or produce ≥80% agreement among knowledgeable human evaluators (WCAG 2.x tightens this to requiring consistent results across independent testers). This is a ready-made bar for what "testable" means in an accessibility acceptance criterion.

- **GOV.UK Service Manual / GDS Way** ([gov.uk/service-manual](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/helping-people-to-use-your-service/making-your-service-accessible-an-introduction), [GDS Way accessibility](https://gds-way.digital.cabinet-office.gov.uk/manuals/accessibility.html)): explicit rule that "accessibility cannot be achieved by adding final touches — it must be considered at all stages," and assigns accessibility ownership by role (content/interaction designers avoid inaccessible patterns, researchers test for it, delivery managers ensure it's considered from the start) — a concrete distribution-of-responsibility model rather than leaving it to one specialist.

### 4. Writing testable, falsifiable accessibility acceptance criteria — the key finding

The most directly applicable pattern is **Deque's "a11yAC" (Accessibility Acceptance Criteria)**, part of their "a11yBID" (Accessibility Behavior-Informed Development) methodology — [Deque: Collaborative planning, the forgotten step of accessible development](https://www.deque.com/blog/collaborative-planning-the-forgotten-step-of-accessible-development/). This is the closest real-world analog to what this pipeline needs:

- a11yAC are written in **Gherkin Given-When-Then** form, same as functional acceptance criteria, and live in the same user story — not a separate a11y appendix.
- Concrete example given:
  > Given I am a blind screen reader user, and I have submitted the form, and a loading spinner is visible as I await a response from the server, When I navigate to the loading spinner image, Then I hear the image role, and I hear the alt text as "loading."
- Explicit design rule: a11yAC should be **agnostic to specific assistive-tech key commands** and instead state the expected *semantics* (role, state, property/name) — i.e., criteria are written against the accessibility-tree contract, not against "press NVDA+X and hear Y," which keeps them stable across AT implementations while remaining falsifiable.
- Process: a "**11y Amigos**" session (analyst/story-writer + developer + tester + designer — a variant of BDD's "three amigos") discovers and documents a11yAC **before development starts**, explicitly because "no single person is expected to know enough about all aspects of accessibility to write quality requirements" — knowledge is distributed across roles rather than assumed to live in one person's head.
- Stated downstream payoff: developers read a11yAC to know what to build and self-test; testers read them to know what to verify; product owners use them as the bar for accepting the story; future maintainers use them to understand why an accessibility-driven implementation choice was made (preventing accidental regression).
- Note: design-specific requirements (contrast, color, spacing) are captured in the visual design artifact itself, not in a11yAC — a11yAC exist specifically to cover what a static visual design cannot express: assistive-technology behavior, states, and announcements.

Complementary: **Deque also runs accessibility heuristic evaluations at the design phase itself** ([Supporting Design: Accessibility Heuristics Evaluation](https://www.deque.com/blog/supporting-the-design-phase-with-accessibility-heuristics-evaluations/)), reinforcing that a11y review belongs at the design/spec review gate, not only at code review.

**WCAG's formal testability bar** (from WebAIM) gives a crisp definition an agent can apply when judging whether a proposed criterion is "testable": it must be answerable objectively (automatable) or reach high inter-rater agreement among evaluators — this is a good litmus test to reject vague criteria like "must be accessible" or "should work with screen readers" in favor of Given-When-Then statements naming a specific role/state/name/behavior.

---

### Synthesis for the pipeline's spec-drafting agents

1. **Treat accessibility acceptance criteria as first-class criteria in the same list as functional ones**, written Given-When-Then, naming assistive-technology-observable semantics (role, name, state, announced text, focus behavior) rather than visual description or vague compliance language — directly modeled on Deque's a11yAC pattern and WCAG's testability bar.
2. **Require an explicit exclusion/persona pass at spec time** ("who could be excluded by this interaction and how does the spec address it") — Microsoft's "recognize exclusion / solve for one, extend to many" gives a concrete prompt shape for this.
3. **Require a stated assistive-tech experience narrative for any new interactive component**, before implementation — BBC's practice of writing the intended screen-reader experience as a design deliverable is a template for a criterion category: "expected AT narrative."
4. **Reject "must be accessible"-style criteria outright** as a spec smell — the whole body of sources (WCAG testability rule, Deque's a11yAC, NN/g's rejection of "checklist" thinking) converges on requiring criteria phrased as falsifiable propositions with a stated verification method (automatable check, or a named evaluator procedure with expected agreement).
5. **Frame accessibility judgment as pragmatic and comparative ("bad to better"), not pass/fail perfectionist** — Heydon Pickering's and A11Y Project's shared stance — useful for an adversarial gate agent (like axiom or canon's auditor) that should flag missing/ambiguous a11y criteria as blockers but not demand an unattainable "100% accessible" bar.
6. **Assign accessibility review to a broadened cast, not a single specialist** — GOV.UK's per-role responsibility model and Deque's "a11y Amigos" both argue against having accessibility live only in one gate agent's judgment; worth reflecting in how the pipeline distributes accessibility-checking responsibility across draft-spec, audit-spec, and gate-spec rather than concentrating it in one late step.</result>

<result># CLI/Terminal Accessibility Research Report

## Headline Finding: No WCAG Equivalent Exists

There is no ratified, industry-standard accessibility specification for CLIs or terminal applications comparable to WCAG. There is no standardized "accessibility tree" analogous to the DOM/ARIA — a terminal is structurally an unstructured text stream (CHI '21 paper, confirmed). What exists is a patchwork: one peer-reviewed study, one widely-cited output-style guide that isn't accessibility-focused (clig.dev), independent practitioner checklists (Seirdy, AFixt), one vendor design-system handbook (PatternFly), and after-the-fact vendor engineering blogs (GitHub, 2025).

## Six Topic Areas, With Checkable Rules

**1. Output streams, machine-readability, exit codes** — stdout for primary output, stderr for diagnostics (clig.dev, confirmed); zero/non-zero exit codes (confirmed); `--json`/`--plain` machine-readable modes (confirmed) — these double as the workaround screen-reader users actually rely on (CHI paper). Key gap: TTY-detection alone can't distinguish "human with screen reader" from "human at plain terminal," so accessibility can't hook into TTY checks alone — it needs explicit flags.

**2. Color** — disable color when not a TTY (clig.dev, confirmed); honor `NO_COLOR` (no-color.org, confirmed) and `FORCE_COLOR` (chalk/supports-color convention, confirmed but not a ratified standard like NO_COLOR); never encode meaning in color alone, pair with text labels (PatternFly, confirmed); constrain color to the 16-color ANSI palette since that's the only range terminals let users remap (GitHub engineering blog, confirmed); support `--color=always|never|auto` (Seirdy, confirmed); treat `TERM=dumb` as strip-all-formatting signal (AFixt, confirmed).

**3. Animation/spinners** — the strongest, most repeated confirmed failure pattern. Animated spinners are "extremely problematic for screen readers" (Seirdy); GitHub CLI's braille-character spinner literally confused screen readers and was replaced with static text (GitHub blog, confirmed); Anthropic's own Claude Code has an open issue (#11002) where NVDA freezes during token-streaming/spinner updates, described as "largely unusable" for accessibility-focused Windows users; even GitHub Copilot CLI's shipped `--screen-reader` mode has a live regression re-announcing a status value on every keypress (cli/copilot-cli#1642) — evidence that shipping a flag isn't sufficient without interaction testing.

**4. Structural semantics** — CLIs lack any accessibility-tree equivalent to HTML/DOM (CHI paper, root cause of most other findings); provide text alternatives for ASCII art, opt-in only via flags (AFixt); box-drawing characters get announced verbosely ("box drawing light horizontal") per Claude Code issue #247 (likely, secondary-source only); unstripped ANSI escape codes get read aloud as literal garbage (likely); man pages' standardized, searchable format is a positive pattern worth preserving (Seirdy).

**5. TUI frameworks — the counter-intuitive core finding.** Bubble Tea (Go) has an open, unresolved "is accessibility on the roadmap" issue with no commitment; Ratatui (Rust) has no confirmed accessibility feature and rendered text can't even be copied from the terminal; Textual (Python), the most accessibility-forward framework surveyed, markets high-contrast/colorblind themes but explicitly describes screen-reader integration as still *planned*, not shipped. One critical (non-peer-reviewed) blog post argues modern canvas-redrawing TUI frameworks can be *worse* than old scrollback CLIs because they redraw the whole screen instead of using VT100 scrolling regions. Terminal emulator choice also matters independently: GTK-based terminals (gnome-terminal, xfce4-terminal) are fully accessible; XTerm, urxvt, st, and Konsole are not (blindcomputing.org, confirmed). **Bottom line: a plain, linear, scrollback-based CLI with a static-text screen-reader mode is currently more accessible than a modern full-screen TUI, not less sophisticated.**

**6. Explicit accessibility modes, testing, documentation** — GitHub's `gh a11y` mode (v2.72.0+) and its 2025 accessibility overhaul (screen-reader mode, colorblind theme picker, keyboard-first nav) is the closest thing to a reference implementation that exists; GitHub's own conclusion is that no single "accessible" format works for everyone — customization via explicit flags is necessary; mandate testing with real screen readers or at minimum piping output through `espeak-ng` and listening (Seirdy); document accessibility flags prominently in `--help`, not a separate doc.

## Honest Gap Assessment

- The one peer-reviewed source (CHI '21, Sampath/Merrick/Macvean, ACM DL) had its full text blocked by a 403 on both fetch attempts — findings from it beyond the abstract are secondary paraphrases, not confirmed direct reads.
- No sustained conference-talk circuit specific to CLI/terminal accessibility was found for 2023–2026; the field runs on one paper, scattered blog posts of uneven rigor, and vendor postmortems rather than proactive research.
- clig.dev, despite being the most-cited CLI guidelines document, has no dedicated accessibility section — its relevance is incidental.

## Recommendation (medium confidence)

Default new CLI/TUI work to plain/static/structured output (topics 1–4, high-confidence, multiply-corroborated); treat any full-screen TUI framework as accessibility-risk-bearing by default and require a static/linear fallback before shipping (topic 5, weaker per-source but strong in aggregate across four independent frameworks); require real screen-reader or espeak-ng testing as a release gate, since every confirmed production failure found (GitHub Copilot CLI, Claude Code) was interactive/behavioral and passed normal code review undetected.</result>
